readings.c3s1:
¶
{{smaller block|The walls of Babylon, . . . so broad that six chariots could well drive together at the top, and so ''battlemented'' that they could not fall. {{right|''Sir T. Herbert'', Travels, p. 228.}}
The old ''battlemented'' walls of the city.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXV. 563.}}}}

'''battle-piece''' (bat′l-pēs), ''n.'' A painting which represents a battle.
{{smaller block|Looking at Crimean ''battle-pieces'', in which French soldiers are shown to have achieved everything, we see exemplified a national sentiment.
{{right|''H. Spencer'', Study of Sociol., p. 214.}}}}

'''battler<sup>1</sup>''' (bat′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''battle''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>; appar. not descended from ME. ''batelur'' (< OF. ''batailleor''), ''batailler'', < OF. ''bataillier''.] One who battles or fights; a warrior or contender.

'''battler<sup>2</sup>†''' (bat′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''battle''<sup>5</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who beats with a bat or battledore.—'''2.''' A bat or beetle.—'''3.''' See ''batler''<sup>1</sup>.

'''battler<sup>3</sup>†''', ''n.'' See ''batteler''.

'''battle-scarred''' (bat′l-skärd), ''a.'' Scarred with wounds received in battle.
{{smaller block|The appeal of a Roman soldier, ''battle-scarred'' in the service of his country, could arouse to vengeance the populace of the great ancient republic. {{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXVI. 60.}}}}

'''battle-shout''' (bat′l-shout), ''n.'' A shout raised in battle.

'''battle-song''' (bat′l-sông), ''n.'' A song sung on the battle-field, or relating to battle; a martial song.
{{smaller block|<poem>The chivalrous ''battle-song''
That she warbled alone in her joy.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, x. 4.}}}}

'''battleton''' (bat′l-ton), ''n.'' [E. dial., appar. a var. of ''battledore''.] Same as ''battledore'', 1.

[Prov. Eng.]

¶
'''battletwig''' (bat′l-twig), ''n.'' [E. dial.] An earwig. [Prov. Eng.] ''Halliwell.''

'''battle-writhen''' (bat′l-riᴛ̵ʜ″en), ''a.'' [< ''battle''<sup>1</sup> + ''writhen'', old pp. of ''writhe''.] Twisted or distorted by stress of battle. [Poetic.]
{{smaller block|His ''battle-writhen'' arms and mighty hands.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}

'''battling†''' (bat′ling), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Also ''batteling''; ppr. and verbal n. of ''battle''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.''] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Nourishing; fattening.
{{smaller block|<poem>The meads environ’d with the silver streams,
Whose ''batt’ling'' pastures fatten all my flocks.</poem>
{{right|''Greene'', Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay.}}}}
'''2.''' Fertile.

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A growing fat, or the process of causing to grow fat; a fattening.—'''2.''' That which nourishes or fattens, as food, or feed for animals, or manure for soil.

'''battological''' (bat-ọ̄-loj′i-kal), ''a.'' [< ''battology'' + ''-ical''.] Given to or of the nature of battology.

'''battologist''' (ba-tol′ọ̄-jist), ''n.'' [< ''battology'' + ''-ist''.] One who talks idly; one who needlessly repeats the same thing in speaking or writing.
{{smaller block|A truly dull ''battologist''.
{{right|''Whitlock'', Manners of Eng. People, p. 209.}}}}

'''battologize''' (ba-tol′ọ̄-jīz), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''battologized'', ppr. ''battologizing''. [< ''battology'' + ''-ize''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To repeat needlessly; iterate. ''Sir T. Herbert.''

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To repeat words or phrases with needless iteration.

'''battology''' (ba-tol′ọ̄-ji), ''n.'' [< Gr. βαττολογία, < βαττολόγος, a stammerer, < βάττος, a stammerer (used only as a proper name), + λέγειν, speak: see ''-ology''.] Idle talk or babbling; a needless repetition of words in speaking. [With reference to Mat. vi. 7.]
{{smaller block|That heathenish ''battology'' of multiplying words.
{{right|''Milton'', Def. of Humb. Remonst.}}
Mere surplusage of ''battology''.
{{right|''Prynne'', Treachery and Disloyalty of Papists, ii. 67.}}}}

'''batton†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''baton'' and ''batten''<sup>2</sup>.

'''battoon†''', ''n.'' Same as ''batoon''.

'''battory†''' (bat′ọ̄-ri), ''n.'' A factory or warehouse established abroad by the Hanse towns.

'''battoule-board''' (ba-töl′bōrd), ''n.'' A spring-board used for jumping—particularly, in circuses, for vaulting over horses, elephants, etc.
{{smaller block|It consists of a few planks fastened at one end to a pole supported by two uprights, the other end resting upon a floor or other surface.}}

'''battril†''' (bat′ril), ''n.'' [E. dial. Cf. ''battler''<sup>2</sup>, ''batler''<sup>1</sup>.] Same as ''batler''<sup>1</sup>.

'''batts''' (bats), ''n. pl.'' Same as ''batting'', 3.

'''battue''' (ba-tū′), ''n.'' [F. (= Pr. ''batuda'' = It. ''battuta''), prop. fem. pp. of ''battre'', beat: see ''bate''<sup>1</sup>, ''batter''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' A method of hunting in which the game is driven from cover by beaters toward a point where the sportsmen are in wait.
{{smaller block|He has not a word to say against ''battue'' shooting, though for his own part he greatly prefers shooting over a well-trained dog to having the game put up in droves by a serried line of beaters.
{{right|''Westminster Rev.'', CXXV. 300.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|battle|479|battue}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|<poem>’Tis ours by craft and by surprise to gain:
’Tis yours to meet in arms and ''battle'' in the plain.</poem>
{{right|''Prior.''}}}}
'''2.''' To struggle; contend; strive for mastery: either absolutely or with ''for'', ''with'', or ''against'': as, to ''battle with'' the winds; to ''battle for'' freedom, or ''against'' adversity; to ''battle with'' ignorance.
{{smaller block|Who ''battled for'' the True, the Just.
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, lvi.}}}}
{{smaller block|Regret, resolve, awe, and joy, every high human emotion excepting fear, ''battled'' about us.
{{right|''E. S. Phelps'', Beyond the Gates, p. 94.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To embattle; put into battle array.—'''2†.''' To fight for.
{{smaller block|Whom thei have seyn alwey ''batailen'' and defenden goode men. {{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, i. prose 4.}}}}
'''3.''' To give battle to; fight against; contend with; fight. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He can ''battle'' theologians with weapons drawn from antique armories unknown to themselves.
{{right|''Whipple'', Ess. and Rev., I. 15.}}}}

'''battle<sup>2</sup>†''' (bat′l), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''battled'', ppr. ''battling''.   [Early mod. E. also ''battel''; < ME. ''bataylen'', ''batailen'', < OF. ''bataillier'', ''bateillier'' (= Pr. ''batalhar''), fortify with battlements, < ''bataille'', battlement, appar. identical with ''bataille'', battle; but in later OF. the verb was merged in ''batillier'', ''bastillier'', < ''bastille'', a fortress: see ''bastile'', ''battle''<sup>1</sup>, and ''battlement'', and cf. ''embattle''<sup>1</sup>, ''embattle''<sup>2</sup>.]   To furnish or strengthen with battlements; embattle.
{{smaller block|<poem>Lest any tyme it were assayed,
Ful wel aboute it was ''batayled''.</poem> {{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 4161.}}}}

'''battle'''<sup>3</sup> (bat′l), ''a.''   [Appears first in the 16th century, in Scotch and North. E., also written ''battel'', ''battil'', ''battill'', ''baittle'', ''bettle'', ''batwell'', etc.; in form < *''bat'', a verbal root appearing in the verb ''batten''<sup>1</sup>, improve, etc., + ''-el'', ''-le'', an adj. formative suffixed to verbal roots, as in ''brittle'', ''fickle'', etc.: see ''batten''<sup>1</sup>, and cf. the later adjectives ''battable'' and ''batful'', appar. modifications of ''battle''<sup>3</sup>.]   In ''agri.'': (''a'') Improving; nutritious; fattening: as, ''battle'' grass; ''battle'' pasture. (''b'') Fertile; fruitful: as, ''battle'' soil; ''battle'' land. [Now only North. Eng. and Scotch.]
{{smaller block|A ''battel'' soil for grain, for pasture good. {{right|''Fairfax.''}}}}

'''battle'''<sup>3</sup>† (bat′l), ''v.''   [Sc. and North. E., also written ''battel'', ''battil'', etc., from the adj. Cf. ''batten''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To nourish; feed.—'''2.''' To render fertile or fruitful, as the soil.
{{smaller block|Ashes are marvellous improvements to ''battel'' barren land. {{right|''Ray’s Proverbs.''}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To grow fat; thrive.
{{smaller block|Sleepe, they sayd, would make her ''battill'' better. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. viii. 38.}}}}
'''2.''' To become fertile or fruitful, as soil.

'''battle<sup>4</sup>†''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''battel''<sup>4</sup>.

'''battle<sup>5</sup>''' (bat′l), ''v. t.''   [Freq. of ''bat''<sup>1</sup> (cf. ''batter''<sup>1</sup>), or perhaps a var. of ''beetle''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', simulating ''bat''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'' (cf. ''bat''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''), or perhaps from ''battledore'', 1, q. v.]   To beat (clothes) with a battler or beetle in washing.

'''battle-ax''' (bat′l-aks), ''n.'' An ax used as a weapon of war. {{smaller|It was in almost universal use before the introduction of firearms, and is still employed among uncivilized peoples. In heraldry it is always represented with a blade on one (usually the dexter) side and a point on the other, the staff terminating in a spear-head.}} {{img float|file=century v01 p0505 c1f1.png|width=181px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Persian Battle-ax, 18th century.}}}}

'''battle-bolt''' (bat′l-bōlt), ''n.'' A bolt or missile of any kind used in battle.
{{smaller block|The rushing ''battle-bolt'' sang from the three-decker.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, i. 13}}}}

'''battle-brand''' (bat′l-brand), ''n.'' A sword used in battle.
{{smaller block|Thy father’s ''battle-brand.''
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., ii. 15}}}}

'''battle-club''' (bat′l-klub), ''n.'' A club used in battle, especially by barbarians, as the South Sea islanders.
{{smaller block|The cursed Malayan crease, and ''battle-clubs'' From the isles of palm.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Prol. to Princess.}}}}

'''battle-cry''' (bat′l-krī), ''n.'' A cry or shout of troops engaged in battle.
{{smaller block|It was evident that their ''battle-cry'' was conquer or die.
{{right|''Thoreau'', Walden, p. 247.}}}}

'''battled<sup>1</sup>''' (bat′ld), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Ranged in battle array; disposed in order of battle.—'''2.''' Contested; fought.
{{smaller block|<poem>Soldier, rest! thy warfare o’er,
Dream of ''battled'' fields no more.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., i. 31.}}}}

'''battled<sup>2</sup>''' (bat′ld), ''a.'' '''1.''' Furnished or strengthened with battlements.
{{smaller block|''Batailled'' as it were a castel wal.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Nun’s Priest’s Tale, l. 40.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''battled'' tower. {{right|''Tennyson'', Fair Women.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''her.'', broken in the form of battlements: said (''a'') of any horizontal line dividing the field; (''b'') of a bar or fesse, when one side only is broken in this way. Also ''embattled.'' See cut under ''embattled.''—{{smaller|'''Battled arrondi,''' in ''her.'', having the heads of the battlements curved or rounded.—'''Battled counter,''' in ''her.'', same as ''counter-embattled.''—'''Battled embattled,''' in ''her.'', doubly battled, or battled in steps. Also called ''grady'' and ''battled grady.''}}

'''battledore, battledoor''' (bat′l-dōr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''batyldore'', ''-doure'', ''-dure''; appar. a modification (simulating *''battle'', as if dim. of ''bat''<sup>1</sup>; cf. ''battle''<sup>5</sup>) of Pr. ''batedor'' (= Sp. ''batidor'', a beater, formerly also ''batador'', a bat for beating clothes—Minsheu), < ''batre'' = Sp. ''batir'', beat: see ''batter''<sup>1</sup>. For the term., cf. ''stevedore.'' Cf. E. dial. ''battleton'', in sense 1.]   '''1.''' A bat or beetle used in washing clothes, or for smoothing them out while being laundered.—'''2.''' An instrument shaped like a racket, but smaller, used in playing the game of battledore and shuttlecock.—'''3†.''' A paddle for a canoe.—'''4.''' In ''glass-making'', a flat square piece of polished iron with a wooden handle, used for flattening the bottoms of tumblers, or for similar purposes.—'''5.''' A kind of paddle with a long handle, used for placing loaves in a baker’s oven.—'''6†.''' A kind of horn-book: so called from its shape.—{{smaller|'''Battledore-boy†''', an abecedarian.—'''Battledore-barley''', a species of cultivated barley, ''Hordeum zeocriton'', with short, broad ears. Also called ''sprat-barley''.   ''N. E. D.''}}

'''battle-field''' (bat′l-fēld), ''n.'' The scene of a battle.
{{smaller block|<poem>Oh! who would fight and march and countermarch,
Be shot for sixpence in a ''battle-field?''</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Audley Court.}}}}

'''battle-flag''' (bat′l-flag), ''n.'' A military flag; a flag carried in battle.
{{smaller block|Till the war-drum throbb’d no longer, and the ''battle-flags'' were furl’d.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Locksley Hall.}}}}

'''battle-ground''' (bat′l-ground), ''n.'' A battle-field.
